newsitem.title: USA: U.S. economy's second-quarter growth revised down slightly.
newsitem.headline: U.S. economy's second-quarter growth revised down slightly.

text.p: The economy expanded at a slightly less robust rate in the second quarter than previously thought, the Commerce Department said on Friday, though it still surged ahead at the fastest rate in two years.

The nation's gross domestic product, or GDP, grew at a 4.7 percent annual rate instead of 4.8 percent in the three months from April through June, the government said in a final revision of second-quarter activity.
The pace of expansion already has begun to slow since mid-year, with most analysts forecasting growth in a range of about 2 percent to 2.5 percent in the final six months of the year.
(May be bylined Glenn Somerville)
The last time the economy grew more vigorously was in the second quarter of 1994, when it boomed ahead at a 4.9 percent annual rate.

The main reason for slightly revising down the second-quarter GDP figure was that federal government spending was not quite as strong as estimated earlier. The Commerce Department said federal spending climbed at a $10.5 billion annual rate instead of $11.9 billion estimated a month ago.
GDP measures the value of all goods and services produced by workers and capital within U.S. borders.
Second-quarter GDP grew at more than twice the rate registered in the first three months of the year, when the economy expanded at a 2 percent annual rate.
Most of the final second-quarter revisions were small and the Commerce Department said they did not significantly change its earlier presentation of national economic activity.

"Growth was markedly higher in the second quarter than the first, and the step-up was mainly accounted for by an upturn in non-farm business inventory investment and by a pickup in state and local governemnt spending," the department said.

The first estimate of third-quarter GDP will not be available for another month. But there already are signs of slowing as consumer spending softens at home and lackluster overseas economies limit foreign sales of U.S.-made goods.
Sales at retail stores barely edged up in July and August. The latest available figures show the U.S. trade balance deteriorated sharply in July as exports weakened.

During the second quarter, businesses increased their inventories by a revised $7.1 billion instead of $7.2 billion estimated a month ago. That followed a $3 billion decrease in stocks of unsold goods during the first quarter and bolstered growth by keepingg
production up.
Consumer spending expanded by 3.4 percent at a $38.5 billion annual rate in the second quarter, the same as estimated a month ago, after growing by 3.5 percent in the first quarter.

There were small upward revisions in second-quarter investment in producers' durable equipment and in net exports. Spending on residential investment shot up by 16.3 percent at a $10.4 billion annual rate in the second quarter, more than twice the 7.4 percent first-quarter increase.

There was no sign of inflation threat. Two inflation measures in the GDP report were left unrevised as the implicit price deflator advanced at a 1.8 percent annual rate, compared with 2.2 percent in the first quarter.
A separate fixed-weights measure of price changes rose 2.2 percent compared with 2.3 percent in the first quarter.
Despite the strong second-quarter economic expansion, corporate profits weakened, falling 0.2 percent from the first quarter to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $408.1 billion.
Department officials said it was the first time in a year that quarterly profits dipped, since they fell 2 percent in the second quarter of 1995.
